questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of a constant-\(g_m\) reference?
options: To generate a bias current that does not depend on the supply voltage, set by a resistor
To give the largest possible current
questions.explanation: The circuit biases itself through a mirror loop. The supply voltage does not appear in the equations, and the resistor sets \(g_m\) (reader Sec. 13.7.1).

questions.prompt: In the constant-\(g_m\) reference, what sets the transconductance of the unit device?
options: Only the resistor and the size ratio: \(g_m = 2(1 - 1/\sqrt K)/R\)
questions.explanation: Equal currents and \(V_{GS3} = V_{GS4} + IR\) give an equation in which \(\mu_nC_{ox}\) cancels from \(g_m\). Process parameters still set the current, but not \(g_m\).

questions.prompt: A constant-\(g_m\) reference has a unit device with \(\mu_nC_{ox}W/L = 1\ \mathrm{mA/V^2}\), \(K = 4\) and \(R = 2\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\). Find the current \(I\) in µA.
questions.explanation: \(V_{ov3} - V_{ov4} = IR\) with \(V_{ov} = \sqrt{2I/k}\) and \(M4\) \(K\) times wider: \(\sqrt{2I/k}(1 - 1/\sqrt K) = IR\), so \(I = 2(1 - 1/\sqrt K)^2/(kR^2) = 2(0.25)/(10^{-3}\cdot4\times10^6) = 125\ \mu\mathrm{A}\).

questions.prompt: Why does a self-biased reference need a start-up circuit?
options: To limit the current at power-up
The zero-current state also satisfies the loop, so it may never turn on
questions.explanation: With every device off, both mirror sides carry zero current consistently. A start-up branch injects a little current to leave that state.

options: It shifts the reference current slightly, a systematic bias error
questions.explanation: Every quantity in the result depends on \(K\); mismatch moves it, much as device mismatch causes amplifier offset.
